claim: The S36 and S37 placement failures at `ci` and `full` scale were caused by card parameters producing parts larger than the `max_data_part_size_bytes = 4194304` routing threshold on the `hot` volume of the `ca_local` and `ca_local3` policies; ClickHouse correctly routed those parts to `ca`.
The multidisk placement policies used by S36 and S37 set `max_data_part_size_bytes` to `4194304` bytes (4 MiB) on their hot volumes.
At `ci` scale, the S36 prefill part is 5.86 MiB and the S37 mixed part is 15.0 MiB, so both exceed the 4 MiB routing threshold and route to `ca`.
At `dev` scale, S36 generates a 0.29 MiB prefill part and S37 generates a 3.75 MiB mixed part, keeping both below the 4 MiB threshold and on local disks.

In S36 run `20260718T002431_S36_seed1`, part `0_0_0_0` was already on disk `ca`, so the initial-local-disk check failed and `MOVE PART ... TO DISK 'ca'` raised `Code 479` because the part was already on `ca`.
S37 verified that the multidisk configuration was applied and that routing itself works: its leg 1 placed a small 2 MiB part on `local1` and a large 20 MiB part on `ca`.
S37 leg 4 failed because all six 15 MiB mixed parts landed on `ca`; the report measured `mixed_bytes_per_part = 15728640` and `route_threshold_bytes = 4194304`.
Every prior green S36 and S37 run was at `dev` scale; the two failures in `RUN_HISTORY.md` were the first runs at `ci` scale.

The `param_table` entries for `ci` and `full` in `cards/s36_s37_disk_move.py` were not threshold-aware: both S36 `rows_per_part*payload_bytes` and S37 `mixed_rows*mixed_payload_bytes` exceeded the 4 MiB routing line.

The preferred S36/S37 fix is to keep placement-check payloads below `ROUTE_THRESHOLD_BYTES` at every scale by increasing part count rather than per-part bytes; raising `max_data_part_size_bytes` is less preferred because it weakens S37's deliberate 4 MiB routing test.

S38 failed twice because no `ref_late_log_detected` event appeared during the 240-second post-injection poll window after injecting a dead-epoch late log at key `.../_log/0000000000000001-fffffffffffffffe`.
After the S38 injection, ch2 completed 40 `Finish/Success` GC rounds while every round reported `CasGcClampSuppressedPasses: 1`, about 284 `DiskS3ReadRequestsErrors`, and `LogError: 1`.

A poison late log causes repeated failing reads that clamp its key, and clamp suppression then skips the orphan-manifest sweep pass that would call `reportLateLogsIfAny`; late-log detection is therefore structurally starved while the clamp persists.
The S38 clamp-starvation condition is fail-closed and does not revive or delete anything, but it violates the observability contract that a late log is reported.

The BACKLOG item `[clamp liveness] scoped suppression under long persistent clamps` should make a clamped key reportable, either by emitting `ref_late_log_detected` or a dedicated clamped-key anomaly directly from the clamp path while the sweep skips the key.

`observe.gc_log_all(cl, since_inject).summary.success` under-counted S38 by returning 0 even though the raw GC log contained 40 post-injection Success rows; a timestamp-format versus `since` comparison is the prime suspected harness cause.

Mount leases and epoch counters already use exact-token deletion plus rechecks, but `OwnerObject` contains only `server_uuid`, so an owner anchor written by a successor reclaiming the same `srid` is indistinguishable from stale debris from the decommissioned server.

T5 replaces deletion of the owner anchor with a conditional in-place tombstone rewrite using `Backend::putOverwrite` and the expected owner token; a successor that changes the object first makes the conditional write fail and the decommission tail aborts closed.
`OwnerObject` gains `std::optional<uint64_t> retired_at_ms`, serialized under the key `"rt"`; the field is absent for an owner that has never been retired.

The decommission tombstone preserves the same `server_uuid`, sets `retired_at_ms` to the current time, and writes it with the prior owner token through `Backend::putOverwrite(owner_key, encodeOwner(...), owner->token)`.

When `claimOwnerOrThrow` finds an owner with the same `server_uuid` but a set `retired_at_ms`, it must throw `CORRUPTED_DATA` with a distinct operator message saying that the identity was explicitly decommissioned and requires deliberately clearing `retired_at_ms` for manual revival.
T5 intentionally adds no new un-decommission CLI flag; manual clearing of `retired_at_ms` is the only revival path in this fix.

The owner-tombstone change requires tests proving that decommission leaves a present owner object with `retired_at_ms` set, that a competing `putOverwrite` makes the tail abort closed, and that a tombstoned same-UUID owner is rejected by `claimOwnerOrThrow` with `CORRUPTED_DATA`.

The T5 tombstone design supersedes only the owner half of the earlier exact-token tail-fencing recommendation; mount and epoch objects continue using exact-token fencing because their values naturally change between incarnations.
The #38 campaign produced a verdict for all 40 scenarios: 27 clean PASS results, 11 scale-limited INCONCLUSIVE results, one real product failure in S38, and the budget-only S08 disposition.
S08's 20000 sequential single-row HTTP INSERTs take about 880–900 seconds at `ci` scale, consuming the default 900-second timeout without stalls; this is a timing budget, not a hang or regression.

`quiesce_cluster` falsely marked S08 inconclusive because it failed immediately on any transient non-empty `replication_queue.last_exception` instead of applying the sibling backlog-stall grace period; commit `35faaae182c` added the grace period and two regression tests.

The 11 campaign INCONCLUSIVE scenarios were pre-existing `ci`-scale instrumentation limitations rather than product bugs, including short GC-log windows, blob-cache masking of fetch counts, unreachable manifest/RSS thresholds, and unavailable compose baselines; full scale is required for final answers.
S36 and S37 passed in the #38 campaign after routing fix `4d457ec378a`, confirming that their prior failures were card scale-parameter errors rather than a product routing regression.
The only unresolved product finding from the #38 campaign was S38 clamp liveness; it was escalated from DESIRABLE to HARD in BACKLOG and requires an architectural scoped-suppression decision.
The CAS review triage confirmed that conditional S3 copy could silently fall back to an unconditional write; task T8 fixed it in commit `a7d171f1d3e`.
The CAS review triage confirmed that swallowed condemn-marker writes could let GC delete a live blob; task T1 fixed the load-bearing gate in commits `21a6051e8ff` and `12ae454e7f2`.

The CAS review triage confirmed that pre-CAS retention pruning based only on proposed generations could permanently wedge GC; task T3 fixed it by using the parent-union-proposed generation set in commit `883c8f92d66`.
The CAS review triage confirmed a scheduler/`cas_store` shutdown use-after-free race and an event-sink assignment/read data race; task T9 fixed both in commit `846a4f62a62`.
The CAS review triage confirmed that `ReaderExecutor` could bypass the `file_view` payload window and return wrong results; task T7 fixed the fallback condition in commit `aaf61086527`.
The CAS review triage confirmed that zero-valued `gc_interval_sec` or `gc_shards` could cause a spin or permanent wedge; task T4 added bounds validation in commit `4fdbb3eaf11`.

The CAS review left CityHash128 without byte verification, local/NFS shared-pool visibility, unknown GCS bucket versioning, the experimental gate for `metadata_type=content_addressed`, `system.content_addressed_mounts` listing errors, and `staging_backend=s3` fallback as open design decisions rather than silent fixes.

Seven ASan gtest findings were test-lifetime bugs rather than product bugs: six stack-use-after-scope cases came from an event-sink vector declared after `Pool`, and `CasPoolShutdown.UnresolvedWedgeSkipsFarewell` had a heap-use-after-free from reading `store->layout()` after `store.reset()`.

The project's `LOGICAL_ERROR` policy reserves it for gross application-invariant violations; ordinary external failures should use an appropriate external-error code, while an external condition that makes ClickHouse state violate an invariant may still be a valid `LOGICAL_ERROR`.

The CAS gtest battery's established `Cas*:CA*:...` filter had never matched about 89–90 tests in the `CaWiring*`, `CaTransaction*`, `CaDedupCache*`, `CaInlinePlacement*`, and `CaPartPathParser*` suites; correcting the filter exposed three bugs in `gtest_ca_wiring.cpp`.

After the filter and test fixes, the complete CAS gtest battery ran with zero exclusions: 1030/1030 plain, 1034/1034 ASan, and 1034/1034 TSan, with four additional death tests present only under `DEBUG_OR_SANITIZER_BUILD`.

Issue [Altinity/ClickHouse#2052](https://github.com/Altinity/ClickHouse/issues/2052) does not reproduce on HEAD because commit `318291fe5e5` moved orphan-manifest ownership recovery to `recoverRefTable`, which `CasOrphanManifestSweep.cpp` still uses through `recoverRefTableDetailed`.

`CasJsonWriter` is intended to replace `WriteBuffer` in all CAS text-format encode paths while preserving byte-identical output; the read side, `JsonObjectReader`, `src/IO/WriteHelpers.h`, and every on-wire byte remain unchanged.

`CasJsonWriter` owns a `String`, appends inline, and supports whole-object assembly for bounded formats plus a reused line-scratch mode for streaming formats; it avoids `WriteBuffer` lifecycle overhead and per-record heap allocations.
The CAS string writer must be the single escaping path for all strings and must not offer a trust-based raw-string shortcut; its semantics are fixed to `escape_forward_slashes = false`.
The `RecordStream` family, including `cas_run`, must remain streaming and bounded by one line (`line_cap` 4 KiB), never by record count.

`CasJsonWriter::stringValue` scans for control bytes, quotes, backslashes, and `0xE2`, bulk-appends safe runs, and preserves the canonical JSON escaping for `\b`, `\f`, `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\u00XX`, U+2028, U+2029, partial `0xE2` sequences, and unescaped `/`.

The `cas_run` writer assembles each NDJSON line in one reused `CasJsonWriter`, performs one bulk `WriteBuffer::write` per line, then calls `clear()` so capacity is retained and memory stays bounded by the largest line.

The CasJsonWriter migration keeps validation such as `checkCanonicalRefName`, `checkManifestRef`, and `checkBudget` in place; `CasJsonWriter` performs no I/O and only propagates `std::bad_alloc` from buffer growth.
The implemented CasJsonWriter migration reduced `BM_EncodeRefLogTxn` from 753 ns to 333 ns, a 2.26× speedup, while preserving byte-identical output.

The benchmark's `BM_MemcpyTxnBytes` floor was 30.7 ns, making the implemented 333 ns encoder about 10.8× the floor rather than the planned ≤3× target; the target was rejected as physically unreachable because a correct encoder must still validate, format numbers, escape JSON, and allocate its buffer.
The accepted CasJsonWriter outcome is the measured 2.26× speedup plus exhaustive byte-identity verification; the memcpy floor remains as a documented benchmark reference, not a pass/fail gate.

The two budget-relevant ref-ledger encodings are pure sums of independent per-row or per-op byte contributions plus O(1) framing: snapshot rows depend only on their own fields, and hypothetical removal operations depend only on owner kind, ref name, and manifest reference.

Before the incremental-budget change, `admits()` fully rebuilt and encoded both a snapshot and a hypothetical whole-namespace removal transaction for every state-growing operation, making a K-op batch against N live refs cost O(K×N).
The pre-change `BM_Admits` benchmark measured 48.8 μs at N=100, 476 μs at N=1,000, 5,018 μs at N=10,000, and 55,976 μs at N=100,000, with an O(N log N) complexity fit.
The 5-hour soak measured approximately 453 ms average caller wait per ref operation in `CasRefQueueWaitMicroseconds / CasRefBatchedMutations`, attributed to the O(N) `admits()` work.

Approach A stores `uint64_t snapshot_body_bytes` and `uint64_t removal_body_bytes` on `RefTableState`; the counters exclude header/meta/trailer framing and the removal transaction's terminal `remove_namespace` operation.
The counters are pure functions of `(committed, precommits)`, so copying a `RefTableState` carries consistent totals without additional synchronization or scans.
The only row-population paths for `RefTableState` are `stateFromSnapshot` and `applyOpInPlace`; these are therefore the only paths that seed or maintain the body-byte counters.

The size helpers `committedRowEncodedSize`, `precommitRowEncodedSize`, `snapshotFramingSize`, `removalOpEncodedSize`, and `removalFramingSize` calculate sizes by using the same encoder fragments as the full formats, avoiding hand-written escaping or length arithmetic.

Counter maintenance covers add precommit, remove precommit, remove committed, promote, and set payload; `set_payload` changes only `snapshot_body_bytes` because the ref name and manifest reference used by removal encoding do not change.

The new `admits()` applies the candidate operation to a scratch state and compares `snapshotFramingSize + snapshot_body_bytes` and `removalFramingSize + removal_body_bytes` against the budgets, reducing a flush batch from O(K×N) to O(K) while preserving the existing preview identifiers and framing.

A debug-only `chassert` recomputes both body totals from scratch after each applied operation, and randomized property tests compare the incremental sizes with full encoder sizes to catch counter drift.

The incremental-budget design rejects a conservative over-estimate because byte-exactness is provable, rejects caching full encoded strings because it would retain two full strings and require line splicing, and rejects reducing `admits()` frequency because it changes per-operation validation granularity.
The incremental `admits()` change does not alter the ref wire format or persisted data and needs no compatibility scaffolding because CAS is pre-release.
A future mutation path that bypasses `applyOpInPlace` would desynchronize the ref-ledger counters; the debug `chassert` is the immediate detector for this invariant violation.
A transient S3 failure during CAS ref-table startup recovery must not permanently strand the table until server restart.

The stuck-table-load design has two layers: `CasRefLedger::ensureRefTableRecovered` retries transient recovery errors with bounded backoff, while CAS tables are placed in a database created with `lazy_load_tables = 1` so a failed load is retried on the next access.

The recovery retry loop runs inside the existing `recovery_in_progress` single-flight guard, catches only `Exception` with `ErrorCodes::NETWORK_ERROR`, and immediately rethrows `CORRUPTED_DATA`, decode errors, `LOGICAL_ERROR`, and the `kRefRecoveryMaxRestarts` brake.
The recovery retry budget defaults are `recovery_retry_budget_ms = 120000`, `recovery_retry_initial_backoff_ms = 1000`, and `recovery_retry_max_backoff_ms = 30000` in `CasRequestBudget`.

Recovery retry backoff is capped exponential, calculated as `min(recovery_retry_max_backoff_ms, recovery_retry_initial_backoff_ms << retry_num)`, and the retry loop re-runs recovery from a fresh `LIST`.

The recovery retry loop releases `rt.state_mutex` before sleeping and re-acquires it afterward; this avoids stalling the whole-store `wedgedRefLaneCount` walk, and the default sleep is interruptible when `fence_ok_fn()` becomes false.
If a failed recovery attempt assigned `rt.state` or `rt.cleanup_markers`, the next retry replays and reassigns them before `rt.recovered` is set, overwriting the partial attempt cleanly.

The retry implementation adds the `CasRefRecoveryRetries` ProfileEvent, distinct from `CasRefRecoveryRestarts`: retries count whole recovery attempts retried after transient object-store errors, while restarts cover a snapshot or log vanishing during reading.
The soak's CAS table is `ca_stress` in the `ca_soak` Atomic database created with `lazy_load_tables = 1`; the table name remains bare and workload connections use `ca_soak` as their default database.

`CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS ca_soak ENGINE = Atomic SETTINGS lazy_load_tables = 1` must run through a default-database connection before any connection whose default database is `ca_soak`, because the latter would fail with `UNKNOWN_DATABASE` on a fresh stand.
A lazily loaded CAS table does not start replication or merges until its first access, so `lazy_load_tables = 1` trades eager startup for retry-on-access behavior.

With `lazy_load_tables = 1`, a table attaches as a `StorageTableProxy`; if its first access fails because RustFS is unavailable, the error is per-query rather than a cached `ASYNC_LOAD_WAIT_FAILED`, and a later access retries without a server restart.

Generic `AsyncLoader` marks a failed async table-load job as terminal and later accesses rethrow the cached exception; `DETACH TABLE` can hit a catch-22 because table resolution waits for the failed job before reaching `eraseAsyncLoadState`.
The only existing retry-on-touch path identified for a failed async table load is the opt-in `lazy_load_tables` mechanism via `StorageTableProxy` (PR #96283, 26.2).

The generic AsyncLoader issue should consider allowing `DETACH TABLE` for a load-`FAILED` table to bypass `waitTableStarted`, or adding an explicit retry-on-touch/system re-trigger for failed table loads; the draft is for manual review and filing, not yet filed.

The incremental `admits()` plan replaces the O(N)-per-operation full re-encode with two running body-byte totals on `RefTableState`, turning a K-op flush batch against an N-ref table from O(K×N) into O(K) with byte-identical decisions.
The incremental-budget implementation maintains `snapshot_body_bytes` and `removal_body_bytes` at five row-mutation sites in `applyOpInPlace` and seeds them once in `stateFromSnapshot`.
The incremental-budget size helpers are factored from the existing snapshot and log encoders so per-row and framing sizes remain byte-identical to full encoding by construction.
A debug-only recompute-and-compare `chassert` and the existing `AdmitsExactnessPropertyTest` are required to detect drift between incremental counters and full encoder sizes.
The incremental-budget change must preserve the snapshot and removal transaction wire formats and requires no `NativeFormat` specification update.

The `admits()` rewrite uses exact framing-size helpers plus the running body counters rather than hand-written delta arithmetic, while preserving the existing `admits` signature and boolean decisions.

The promote-path counter decrement may occur before a later validation exception because `applyRefLogTxn` mutates a scratch copy and installs it only after the whole transaction succeeds; the partially updated scratch state is discarded on failure.
